name: Femoroacetabular Impingement Syndrome (FAIS)
summary: Symptomatic nonarthritic hip condition involving motion-related hip/groin pain with clinical findings and cam/pincer morphology when imaging is relevant.

redFlags: Neurologic symptoms not explained by hip
firstSteps: Hip and trunk mobility where truly restricted

assess: Reduced hip internal rotation/flexion in some patients

tests.name: FADIR
tests.purpose: Provocative test for intra-articular/nonarthritic hip pain including FAIS.

tests.name: FABER / Patrick
tests.purpose: Assess hip/SI-region symptom provocation and mobility.
tests.positive: Groin pain suggests hip involvement; posterior pain may implicate SI-region structures.

stages.label: Modify Provocation & Restore Motion
stages.goal: Reduce repeated impingement-provoking load while maintaining activity.
do: Hip and trunk mobility where truly restricted
dose: Isometric/low-load hip abduction, extension, rotation: 3 x 8–15 or 3–5 holds

stages.label: Strength & Movement Coordination
stages.goal: Increase hip/trunk capacity and improve task mechanics.

stages.label: Sport / Deep-Flexion Exposure
stages.goal: Restore required range and loading tolerance.
do: Graded pivoting, running and deep-flexion exposure

mechanism: Repeated deep hip flexion/adduction/internal rotation exposure
Morphology plus load and movement factors
investigations: Diagnosis combines symptoms, examination and imaging morphology when required.
Radiographs are commonly first-line imaging if FAIS is suspected; MRI may evaluate labrum/cartilage.
manual: Joint mobilization may be used when pain/capsular restriction limits mobility.
Soft-tissue techniques may be used when muscle/fascial restriction contributes to motion loss.
Avoid repeatedly forcing painful impingement range.
modalities: Use symptom-relieving options only if they help participation in active rehabilitation.
mistakes: Treating imaging morphology rather than symptoms/function
pearls: FADIR reproduces symptoms but does not by itself diagnose FAIS.
A multimodal program of activity modification, strengthening, movement training and selective manual therapy is supported.

tests.name: FADIR
tests.purpose: Provocative test for intra-articular/nonarthritic hip pain including FAIS.
procedure: Flex hip toward about 90° or tolerated range.
Ask if familiar groin pain is reproduced.
tests.interpretation: Sensitive provocative finding for intra-articular hip pathology; not specific enough to diagnose FAIS alone.

tests.name: FABER / Patrick
tests.purpose: Assess hip/SI-region symptom provocation and mobility.
tests.positive: Groin pain suggests hip involvement; posterior pain may implicate SI-region structures.
tests.patientPosition: Supine; tested ankle placed above opposite knee in figure-four position.
tests.handPlacement: One hand stabilizes opposite pelvis/ASIS; the other gently lowers tested knee.
procedure: Place hip in flexion, abduction and external rotation.
Apply gentle downward pressure at knee if needed.
tests.interpretation: Useful as part of differential assessment, not a standalone FAIS diagnosis.

story.headline: A hip pinch, a deep squat and a misleading positive test
story.scene: A young weightlifter says deep squats create a pinch in the groin. A video says one FADIR test can 'diagnose a cam.' The clinician quietly puts away the crystal ball.
story.dialogue: Lifter: 'FADIR hurt. So I definitely need surgery?' Therapist: 'One painful test doesn't get to write the whole ending.'
story.clue: FAI syndrome involves symptoms, compatible examination and relevant imaging findings. Hip morphology alone can be present in people without symptoms.
story.twist: A positive FADIR reproduces pain but is not specific for FAIS. Consider hip OA, labral-related problems, lumbar referral and other causes as appropriate.
story.aha: A shape on a scan is not the same as a painful syndrome.
story.patientTranslation: Some hip positions may bring tissues into an uncomfortable range. We'll look at your symptoms, movement and imaging if needed, then build a plan for the activities you value.
story.clinicianReasoning: Apply the symptoms–signs–imaging framework for FAIS rather than labeling from morphology or FADIR alone. Screen red flags and alternative diagnoses, modify provocative positions and strengthen with movement retraining.
story.rehabBridge: Adjust painful depth and training load → rebuild hip/trunk strength and movement options → graded return to squatting or sport.
story.question: A lifter has groin pain and a positive FADIR test. What is required before diagnosing FAIS?
options: Use the positive FADIR as definitive proof
Treat any cam shape on imaging even when asymptomatic
Integrate symptoms, examination, relevant imaging and differential assessment
story.explanation: FAI syndrome is diagnosed from concordant symptoms, clinical signs and imaging—not a single provocative test.
